description: Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole is a culinary jewel from Oaxaca, Mexico, renowned for its profound complexity and rich, dark hue. This traditional sauce masterfully blends a variety of dried chiles, spices, nuts, seeds, and Mexican chocolate to create an unforgettable taste experience. It transforms any meal into a celebration of authentic Mexican flavors.

instructions.title: Prepare and Toast Chiles
instructions.text: Lightly toast the dried chiles in a dry skillet over medium heat for 30-60 seconds per side until fragrant but not burnt. Be careful not to over-toast, as they can become bitter. Transfer them to a bowl and cover with hot water. Let them soak for 15-20 minutes until softened, then drain and reserve some soaking liquid.

instructions.title: Roast Aromatics and Toast Spices
instructions.text: In the same skillet, dry roast tomatillos, tomatoes, onion, and garlic until softened and slightly charred. Set aside. In a separate dry skillet, lightly toast almonds, peanuts, sesame seeds, raisins, cinnamon stick, cloves, peppercorns, and anise seeds until fragrant. Be careful not to burn. Break the tortilla into pieces and lightly toast or fry until crisp.

instructions.title: Blend Ingredients
instructions.text: Combine the softened chiles, roasted vegetables, toasted nuts, seeds, spices, raisins, and tortilla pieces in a blender. Add 1 cup of chicken broth and blend until a very smooth paste forms. You may need to add a little more broth or reserved chile soaking liquid to achieve a smooth consistency. Strain the mixture through a fine-mesh sieve into a bowl, pressing firmly to extract all liquid and discarding any solids.

instructions.title: Fry the Mole Paste
instructions.text: Heat the vegetable oil in a large pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Carefully pour the strained mole paste into the hot oil. It will splatter, so be cautious. Cook the paste, stirring constantly, for 10-15 minutes, allowing it to darken and thicken. This step is crucial for developing the deep flavor of the mole.

instructions.title: Simmer the Mole
instructions.text: Gradually stir in the remaining 3 cups of chicken broth into the fried mole paste, ensuring it is well combined and smooth. Add the chopped Mexican chocolate and sugar. Bring the mixture to a gentle simmer, then reduce the heat to low, cover, and cook for at least 20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the chocolate has melted and the mole has thickened to your desired consistency. The longer it simmers, the more the flavors meld.

instructions.title: Season and Serve
instructions.text: Taste the mole and adjust seasoning with salt and additional sugar if needed. The mole should have a balance of savory, sweet, and spicy flavors. Serve the Mole Negro hot, typically over poached or roasted chicken, with a side of white rice and warm tortillas. Garnish with a sprinkle of sesame seeds.

tips: Always toast your chiles and spices carefully; burning them will result in a bitter mole. A dry skillet over medium-low heat is best for even toasting.
For an extra layer of flavor, consider adding a piece of plantain or a few prunes to the blender with the other ingredients. This adds sweetness and depth.
Mole Negro improves with age. Make it a day ahead and gently reheat it on the stovetop, adding a splash of broth if it has thickened too much.
article:
The aroma alone tells a story: deep, earthy, smoky, with whispers of chocolate and spice. This is the magic of Oaxacan Black Mole, a culinary masterpiece that stands as a testament to Mexico's rich gastronomic heritage. More than just a sauce, Mole Negro is an experience, a complex symphony of flavors that has captivated palates for centuries. If you're exploring Mexican dinner recipes, preparing an authentic Oaxacan Black Mole is an unparalleled journey into the heart of traditional Mexican cuisine.

## What is Oaxacan Black Mole?

Oaxacan Black Mole, known in Spanish as Mole Negro, is arguably the most famous and complex of all the moles from the Mexican state of Oaxaca. Often referred to as "the king of moles," its distinctive dark, almost black color and incredibly layered flavor profile set it apart. This isn't a dish you whip up in a hurry; it's a labor of love, a slow-cooked culinary event that traditionally involves 20 to 30 or even more ingredients. The resulting sauce is a harmonious blend of smoky chiles, rich spices, nuts, seeds, fruits, and a touch of unsweetened Mexican chocolate, creating a balance of sweet, savory, spicy, and earthy notes that is simply unforgettable. While other moles exist in Oaxaca – like mole coloradito, mole amarillo, and mole verde – Oaxacan Black Mole holds a special place, often reserved for significant celebrations, weddings, and holidays, symbolizing tradition and abundance.

## Ingredients for Authentic Mole Negro

The sheer number of ingredients in Oaxacan Black Mole can seem daunting, but each plays a crucial role in building its iconic flavor and texture. Understanding these components is the first step in appreciating this incredible Mexican dinner recipe.

*   **The Chiles:** These are the soul of Oaxacan Black Mole. A specific blend is essential, including chilhuacle negro (the most traditional and hardest to find, contributing to the dark color and deep fruitiness), mulato, ancho, and pasilla chiles. These are toasted, rehydrated, and often charred to develop their smoky depth and contribute to the sauce's dark hue.
*   **Spices:** Aromatic spices infuse the mole with warmth and complexity. Expect cinnamon sticks, cloves, black peppercorns, cumin seeds, anise seeds, thyme, oregano, and sometimes marjoram.
*   **Nuts and Seeds:** These provide body, richness, and nutty undertones. Almonds, peanuts, sesame seeds, and pumpkin seeds are commonly used, toasted to enhance their flavor.
*   **Fruits and Sweeteners:** To balance the heat and earthiness, ingredients like plantains, raisins, prunes, and a touch of piloncillo (unrefined cane sugar) or brown sugar are often included, adding a subtle sweetness and fruity notes.
*   **Thickeners and Aromatics:** Stale tortillas or bread (like bolillo) are often fried and added for thickening. Garlic, onion, and sometimes roasted tomatoes or tomatillos contribute foundational savory flavors.
*   **Mexican Chocolate:** This is a non-negotiable ingredient, but it's crucial to use unsweetened or very dark Mexican chocolate. It doesn't make the mole taste like candy; rather, it deepens the color, adds a subtle bitterness, and enhances the overall complexity, rounding out the flavors without making it sweet.
*   **Broth:** Chicken or turkey broth is typically used to achieve the desired consistency and add another layer of savory richness.

## Step-by-Step Guide to Making Oaxacan Black Mole

Making Oaxacan Black Mole is a multi-stage process, but each step builds towards the final, glorious result. Patience and attention to detail are your best allies.

1.  **Prepare the Chiles:** Start by carefully toasting the dried chiles in a dry comal or skillet until fragrant, being careful not to burn them. Some recipes also call for briefly charring them. Remove stems and seeds (saving some seeds for charring if desired), then rehydrate them in hot water until softened.
2.  **Toast and Fry Other Ingredients:** In batches, toast the nuts and seeds until golden. Separately, fry the plantain, raisins, prunes, and the stale bread/tortilla pieces until lightly browned. Sauté the garlic, onion, and any fresh tomatoes or tomatillos until softened and slightly caramelized.
3.  **Char the "Ash":** This is a traditional step for Oaxacan Black Mole. Some of the reserved chile seeds, along with a small piece of tortilla or bread, are charred until almost black, then ground into a fine ash. This contributes to the mole's distinctive dark color and subtle bitter notes.
4.  **Blend Everything:** This is where the magic starts to come together. In batches, blend the rehydrated chiles with some of their soaking liquid until very smooth. Then, add the toasted nuts, seeds, fried fruits, bread, aromatics, spices, and the charred ash, blending each component thoroughly, adding broth as needed, until you have several smooth, thick pastes.
5.  **Cook the Mole:** Heat a generous amount of lard or oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven. Carefully pour in the blended chile paste, stirring constantly to prevent sticking. This frying step is crucial for developing the flavors and color. Gradually add the other blended pastes, stirring well after each addition.
6.  **Simmer and Season:** Once all the pastes are combined, stir in the chicken or turkey broth. Bring the mixture to a gentle simmer. Add the Mexican chocolate, stirring until it's fully melted and incorporated. Now comes the long simmer – at least 1-2 hours, stirring frequently, to allow the flavors to meld and deepen. The mole should be thick but pourable. Season with salt and piloncillo/brown sugar to taste, adjusting the balance of sweet, savory, and spicy.

## Tips for the Best Mole Negro

*   **Source Quality Ingredients:** The success of your Oaxacan Black Mole hinges on the freshness and quality of your ingredients, especially the chiles. Seek out authentic Mexican ingredients if possible.
*   **Patience is Key:** This is not a quick meal. Give yourself ample time for each step, especially the toasting, blending, and simmering. Rushing will compromise the depth of flavor.
*   **Don't Burn the Chiles:** Toasting should bring out their aroma, not turn them acrid. A quick toast on a dry comal is usually sufficient before rehydrating.
*   **Blend Thoroughly:** For the silkiest Oaxacan Black Mole, blend your ingredients until absolutely smooth. You might need to strain the mole through a fine-mesh sieve at the end if you don't have a high-powered blender.
*   **Taste and Adjust:** Mole is all about balance. Continuously taste your mole during the simmering process and adjust the seasoning – a pinch more salt, a touch more piloncillo, or even a splash of broth can make a significant difference.
*   **Make Ahead:** Mole, like many stews, often tastes even better the next day as the flavors have more time to marry and deepen.

## Serving Suggestions for Mole Negro

Once your Oaxacan Black Mole is perfected, the ways to enjoy it are endless. It is truly a versatile Mexican dinner recipe that can elevate any meal.

*   **With Poultry:** The most traditional pairing is with cooked chicken or turkey. Simply simmer pieces of cooked poultry in the mole until heated through and coated.
*   **Enmoladas:** Spoon the mole over cheese-filled enchiladas (enmoladas) for a rich and comforting vegetarian option.
*   **Tamales:** Use Oaxacan Black Mole as the filling for tamales, or serve it alongside them.
*   **Pork or Duck:** While less common than chicken, mole negro also pairs beautifully with slow-cooked pork shoulder or roasted duck.
*   **Vegetarian Feast:** Drizzle it over roasted sweet potatoes, grilled portobello mushrooms, or even a hearty bowl of rice and beans for a flavorful plant-based meal.
*   **Accompaniments:** Always serve with warm corn tortillas for scooping up every last drop, and a side of Mexican rice and black beans. Garnish with a sprinkle of toasted sesame seeds or fresh cilantro for added texture and freshness.

## Storage and Reheating Tips

One of the great advantages of making a large batch of Oaxacan Black Mole is its excellent storage capabilities.

*   **Refrigeration:** Leftover mole can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5-7 days. Its flavors will often deepen and improve over this time.
*   **Freezing:** Mole freezes exceptionally well. Divide it into individual or family-sized portions and store in freezer-safe containers or bags for up to 3-6 months. This makes the effort of making a big batch even more worthwhile, providing delicious Mexican dinner recipes on demand.
*   **Reheating:** To reheat, gently warm the mole on the stovetop over low heat, stirring occasionally. If it has thickened too much in the refrigerator or freezer, add a little chicken broth or water to reach your desired consistency. Avoid boiling vigorously, as this can alter the delicate balance of flavors.

Embarking on the journey of making Oaxacan Black Mole is an act of culinary devotion. It's a dish that connects you to generations of tradition, offering not just a meal, but a profound cultural experience. Whether you create it from scratch or seek out an authentic version, this iconic Mexican dinner recipe promises a depth of flavor that few other dishes can rival.
